_doc: Phase 379. One row per item where the nano-ros user API does NOT correspond
to the ROS 2 client library it mirrors. Written by hand; read by
`scripts/api-parity.py --check`, which fails on any non-matching row that has
no entry here.
Key is '<lang>:<normalized item>' exactly as the report prints it, where lang
is one of c / cpp / rust. Run the report to get the spelling; do not guess it.
verdict is one of:
divergence  we changed it and a PLATFORM CONSTRAINT is why. `why` must name
the constraint (no_std, no exceptions, no allocator, no runtime
env, single-threaded transport) -- not a preference. This is the
only sanctioned reason to differ (RFC-0036).
extension   we add it because an RTOS scenario needs it; ROS 2 has none.
declined    ROS 2 has it, we deliberately do not, with the reason.
gap         ROS 2 has it, we should too, nobody has done it. A gap is a
legitimate entry -- the point is that it is written down.
rename      the names differ and OURS is the one that should change. A
rename with no platform reason costs the drop-in claim for
nothing, so these are the campaign's work list.
This file is SEEDED, not complete: W1 shipped the correlator, W2 classifies
the rest. `--check` is deliberately not wired into `just check` until then --
a gate that fails on ~2000 rows from the day it lands is one somebody
switches off. Keys beginning with '_' are documentation and are skipped.
the `<lang>:` rows for its own lane, and `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every
shard in this directory. One agent per lane can write without a rebase
conflict against the others.
SHARDED BY TOPIC: this file holds one stage's rows in ALL THREE
languages, because the campaign closes a feature at a time across every
language. `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every shard here, and
`--self-test` rejects a row whose item belongs to a different stage.

c:client_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl; our handles carry their state inline. See `c:publisher_impl_t`.

c:client_init_best_effort.why: rclc ships an entry point per QoS preset; ours takes a QoS value. See `c:publisher_init_best_effort`.

c:client_init_default.why: rclc's default-QoS wrapper; `nros_client_init` IS the default form. See `c:publisher_init_default`.

c:client_init_polling.why: RFC-0022's polling tier. See the pubsub stage's `cpp:PollingSubscription`.

c:client_service_is_ready.why: the correctly-named half of `c:client_server_available`, present only in C. Keeping both is the defect; see that row.

c:client_set_response_callback.why: the reply arrives at a callback bound to the CLIENT at creation, rather than resolving a future. `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` and RFC-0041, on the client side.

c:client_set_timeout.why: a per-client default deadline for a pending request, so a device that must not wait forever states the bound once rather than at every call. rclcpp has no client-level timeout -- the caller passes one to `spin_until_future_complete` each time.

c:client_wait_for_service.why: blocks until the server appears or the deadline passes, driving the executor. rclcpp's `Client::wait_for_service` folds onto ours by the *Base rule; C's rclc has no counterpart.

c:executor_register_parameter_services.why: registers the six `rcl_interfaces/srv/*` servers on the executor as one call. rclcpp starts them from `NodeOptions::start_parameter_services` at node construction; ours is explicit because the six queryables are a measurable cost against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) and an image that does not need them should not pay.

c:send_response.why: rcl's free-function spelling; ours is the method-style `nros_service_send_response`. Same shape as `c:publish` -- the word matches, the spelling is ours to align.

c:take_request.why: rcl's free-function spelling of a word our C already uses: `nros_service_take_request`. Note this makes the pubsub stage's `take` -> `try_recv` rename internally inconsistent as well -- C says TAKE for a service request and TRY_RECV for a subscription, while C++ says `try_recv_request` for both. Whatever W5 picks has to be picked once, for every entity and every language.

c:take_response.why: the client side of `c:take_request`; ours is `nros_client_try_recv_response` -- so within the C API a service TAKES and a client TRY_RECVs. Same one decision.

cpp:Client::async_send_request.why: rclcpp returns a `std::shared_future` a caller `get()`s, and `spin_until_future_complete` drives the executor underneath. Ours returns a `Promise` the caller drives explicitly (`promise.wait(&mut executor, timeout)`) -- RFC-0021. needs a future and a runtime to await it. RFC-0021 makes every blocking helper take the executor and drive it (`promise.wait(&mut executor, timeout)`), which is what makes a timeout reliable on a single-threaded transport. The arity matches by coincidence, which is why the correlator files it `arity-only`.

cpp:Client::prune_pending_requests.why: rclcpp lets a caller drop requests whose replies will never arrive, because each pending request holds a promise until it is answered. Ours has a per-client timeout (`nros_client_set_timeout`) and no way to abandon a specific outstanding request, so a client that gave up still occupies its slot until the deadline. Bounded by the static request table rather than unbounded as in rclcpp -- but a device that retries has no way to reclaim early. Phase 379 W3.

cpp:Service::send_response.why: rcl, rclcpp and rclrs all say send_response. Our C says `nros_service_send_response` -- correctly -- while our C++ says `Service::send_reply` and our Rust says `ServiceTrait::send_reply`. Worse, C contradicts ITSELF: `nros_service_send_response` sits beside `nros_service_send_reply_raw`. Three languages, two words, and one of them uses both. Nothing about an RTOS prefers either. Settle on `send_response` and move `send_reply`, `send_reply_raw` and `ServiceTrait::send_reply` to it. Phase 379 W5.

rust:Client.why: rclrs's `Client` is a handle a node hands back. Ours splits in two: `ServiceClient`, the entity a component DECLARES, and `ClientTrait`, the RMW seam a backend implements. entities are DECLARED by a component rather than created on a live node (RFC-0043/0044); see the node stage's `rust:Node`.

rust:Client::service_name.why: see `cpp:Client::get_service_name` -- rclrs has this and our Rust client does not either.

rust:ClientDispatch::call_raw.why: the generated dispatch path for a raw client call. Machinery `nros::node!` expands into; see issue 0784.

rust:ClientOptions.why: rclrs's client options carry QoS and a callback group; ours carry QoS. See `compile-time-options`.

rust:ClientOutput.why: needs a future and a runtime to await it. RFC-0021 makes every blocking helper take the executor and drive it (`promise.wait(&mut executor, timeout)`), which is what makes a timeout reliable on a single-threaded transport. rclrs's channel for delivering a reply to whichever of its three call shapes was used.

rust:ClientTrait.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend. Exported from `nros::` alongside the user API, which is issue 0784's complaint.

rust:ClientTrait::poll_server_discovery.why: advances discovery a step without blocking, so a polling task can wait for a server without giving up its loop. rclrs waits on a future.

rust:ClientTrait::send_request.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend. Exported from `nros::` alongside the user API, which is issue 0784's complaint.

rust:ClientTrait::server_available.why: a THIRD spelling of the same predicate, in the same trait as `is_server_ready`. See `cpp:Client::service_is_ready`.

rust:EmbeddedServiceClient.why: part of the IMPERATIVE Rust API, which coexists with the declarative component model and is the rclrs-shaped one: `NodeHandle` (exported from `nros` and IN THE PRELUDE, behind `rmw-cffi`) hands back concrete entities you hold and call. rclrs's counterpart exists and correlates by concept but not by name, because ours carries the storage strategy in the type -- `Embedded*` means the entity lives in the executor's static table rather than behind an `Arc`, which is the no-allocator constraint made visible in the name. Whether the two Rust APIs should both be public, and which one `nros::` should lead with, is issue 0784.

rust:QoSProfile::parameter_services_defa.why: the parameter services use a distinct QoS profile in ROS 2 (transient-local, so a late-joining tool still sees declared parameters). We register the parameter servers with the plain services profile, so a tool that starts after the device will not see them until it asks again. Phase 379 W3; see the param stage.

rust:QoSProfile::services_default.why: rclrs spells the preset `QoSProfile::services_default`; ours is `QosSettings::services_default` -- the same words on a type we spell `QosSettings` where ROS 2 spells `QoSProfile`. The type rename belongs to the qos stage; this row records that the preset itself lines up.

rust:RawServiceCallback.why: the raw-bytes callback type; see the pubsub stage's `rust:RawSubscriptionCallback`.

rust:RequestId.why: rclrs wraps `rmw_request_id_t` -- a writer GUID plus a sequence number -- so a reply can be correlated across a restart. Ours is a bare `i64` sequence number scoped to the entity, because the entity table is static and a request cannot outlive its client. Cheaper, and it cannot express a reply to a client that has been recreated.

rust:ServiceClient::service_hash.why: the type hash used to detect a client and server built against different .srv definitions. ROS 2 Iron+ computes one; Humble does not (RFC-0036 records `TYPE_HASH = TypeHashNotSupported`), so this is ours for now and a convergence point when the baseline moves.

rust:ServiceClient::service_type.why: the ROS service type name a declared entity carries, so codegen and the launch resolver can check both ends agree without running the image (RFC-0043). rclrs knows the type statically and never needs it as data.

rust:ServiceHandle.why: rclrs's rcl handle wrapper; ours is an index into the executor's static entity table. See the pubsub stage's `rust:PublisherHandle`.

rust:ServiceInfo::new.why: identity a declared service carries so the launch resolver can attribute it -- domain, namespace, declaring node. rclrs answers the same questions at runtime by querying the graph, which needs discovery.

rust:ServiceRequest.why: what a service callback receives: the request plus the sequence number its reply must carry. rclrs passes the request and an `rmw_request_id_t` separately. See `rust:RequestId`.

rust:ServiceServer.why: entities are DECLARED by a component rather than created on a live node (RFC-0043/0044); see the node stage's `rust:Node`.

rust:ServiceServer::name.why: entities are DECLARED by a component rather than created on a live node (RFC-0043/0044); see the node stage's `rust:Node`.

rust:ServiceServer::new.why: entities are DECLARED by a component rather than created on a live node (RFC-0043/0044); see the node stage's `rust:Node`.

rust:ServiceTag.why: names a declared service so a component's single `on_callback` can tell which one fired (RFC-0043). See the pubsub stage's `rust:SubscriptionTag`.

rust:ServiceTrait.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend. Exported from `nros::` alongside the user API, which is issue 0784's complaint.

rust:ServiceTrait::handle_request.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend. Exported from `nros::` alongside the user API, which is issue 0784's complaint.

rust:ServiceTrait::has_request.why: non-destructive readiness check so a polling task can decide whether to take. See the pubsub stage's `rust:Subscription::has_data`.

rust:ServiceTrait::send_reply.why: see `cpp:Service::send_response` -- the third of our three languages, and the second to say `reply`.
